painstaking.definition: done with great care, thoroughness, and attention to detail
sentences: After years of painstaking research in the archives, the historian finally verified every date and name in her biography of the obscure poet.
The restorer's painstaking work on the fresco, done one square centimeter at a time, took nearly three years to complete.
painstaking.mnemonic: Peine + taking : il faut se donner de la peine pour le faire.

punctilious.definition: showing great attention to correct behavior, etiquette, and small details
sentences: The punctilious butler never forgot a single rule of protocol, correcting the guests whenever they placed a fork or addressed a duchess improperly.
Known for being punctilious about deadlines and formatting, the editor returned the manuscript because the margins were a quarter inch too narrow.
punctilious.mnemonic: Vient de « point » : il s'attache au moindre point de détail.

exacting.definition: demanding great effort, precision, or high standards
sentences: Her exacting supervisor rejected the report three times, insisting that every figure be checked against the original data before submission.
Surgery is an exacting profession that leaves no room for carelessness, since even a tiny error can have fatal consequences.
exacting.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « exact » seulement, mais qui exige l'exactitude.

stringent.definition: strict, severe, and rigorously enforced (of rules or requirements)
sentences: The government imposed stringent safety regulations on the factory after the explosion, and inspectors now visit every month without warning.
Because admission standards at the conservatory are so stringent, only a handful of the hundreds of applicants are accepted each year.
stringent.mnemonic: Même racine que « stringer » / « astreindre » : on serre la vis.

cursory.definition: hasty and superficial, done without attention to detail
sentences: The inspector gave the wiring only a cursory glance, so he missed the frayed cable that later started the fire.
A cursory reading of the contract suggested it was fair, but a careful review revealed several clauses that favored the seller.
cursory.mnemonic: Du latin « currere », courir : on court sur le texte.

perfunctory.definition: done as a routine duty, with little interest or genuine effort
sentences: The clerk gave a perfunctory nod without looking up from his screen, clearly uninterested in the customer's complaint.
Her perfunctory apology, delivered in a flat voice and without eye contact, convinced no one that she regretted her remarks.

haphazard.definition: lacking order, planning, or method; random
sentences: The books were arranged in such a haphazard way, with novels beside cookbooks and atlases, that finding anything took hours.
Critics blamed the haphazard planning of the city's roads for the daily gridlock, noting that no one had coordinated the projects.
haphazard.mnemonic: Hap = hasard : ça se fait au hasard.

shoddy.definition: poorly made or done; of low quality
sentences: The tenants complained about the shoddy construction of the building, noting that the walls cracked and the pipes leaked within a year.
Shoddy workmanship ruined the reputation of the company, as customers discovered that its furniture collapsed after only a few months.

desultory.definition: lacking a plan or purpose; jumping from one thing to another
sentences: The conversation at the dinner party was desultory, drifting from politics to gardening to football without any thread connecting the topics.
After losing his job, he made only desultory efforts to find another, sending a résumé now and then but never following up.
desultory.mnemonic: Latin « desultor » : cavalier qui saute d'un cheval à l'autre.

sentences: Fresh fruit was plentiful at the market that summer, so vendors sold peaches at half the usual price and still made a profit.
In regions where rain is plentiful, farmers rarely worry about drought, whereas those in arid zones must ration every drop of water.

replete.definition: filled to the brim; abundantly supplied (with)
sentences: The old library was replete with rare manuscripts, its shelves so crowded that some volumes were stacked on the floor.
Her memoir, replete with vivid anecdotes and unexpected humor, kept readers engaged from the first page to the very last.
replete.mnemonic: Ressemble à « replet » en français : bien rempli, plein.

rife.definition: widespread and common, especially of something undesirable
sentences: Rumors were rife in the office after the sudden resignation, and employees whispered about layoffs and scandal in every corridor.
The early industrial city was rife with disease, since crowded housing and polluted water allowed infections to spread unchecked.

surfeit.definition: an excessive amount of something, often causing disgust
sentences: After the holiday feast, the guests suffered a surfeit of rich food and could hardly look at another dessert.
A surfeit of cheap imports flooded the market, driving prices down so far that local producers could no longer cover their costs.
surfeit.mnemonic: Sur + fait : on en a trop fait, trop mangé.

inordinate.definition: unreasonably or excessively great; out of proportion
sentences: The committee spent an inordinate amount of time debating the color of the logo while ignoring the project's serious budget problems.
He took an inordinate pride in his small garden, mentioning it in every conversation and boasting to anyone who would listen.
inordinate.mnemonic: In + ordinaire : hors de l'ordre, hors mesure.

slew.definition: a large number or quantity of something
sentences: The new policy provoked a slew of complaints from residents, who flooded the mayor's office with calls and emails within hours.
She returned from the conference with a slew of ideas, filling three notebooks with proposals for improving the department.

swathe.definition: a broad strip or large area of something
sentences: The wildfire cut a wide swathe through the forest, leaving a broad strip of blackened trees that stretched for miles.
A large swathe of the electorate remained undecided until the final week, leaving pollsters unable to predict the outcome.

burgeon.definition: to grow or increase rapidly; to flourish
sentences: Once a sleepy fishing village, the town began to burgeon after the railroad arrived, and its population tripled within a decade.
Her interest in astronomy burgeoned during adolescence, so that by eighteen she was reading graduate-level textbooks and building telescopes.
burgeon.mnemonic: Ressemble à « bourgeon » : ça pousse vite.

sentences: The detectives had scant evidence against the suspect, only a single blurry photograph and a vague description from one witness.
Paying scant attention to the lecture, he scribbled in his notebook and was unable to answer the professor's simple question.

scarce.definition: insufficient in supply; rare and hard to find
sentences: During the drought, clean water became scarce, and families had to walk several miles each morning to fill their buckets.
Jobs for historians are scarce, so many graduates with doctorates compete for a handful of university positions every year.

sparse.definition: thinly scattered or spread out; not dense
sentences: The desert vegetation was sparse, with only a few shrubs scattered across miles of bare, cracked earth.
Because the population of the mountain region is sparse, the nearest hospital can be a two-hour drive from many villages.

paltry.definition: so small or worthless as to be insulting or trivial
sentences: The workers were outraged by the paltry raise of two dollars a month, which did not even cover the rising price of bus fares.
He sold the antique desk for a paltry sum, never realizing that collectors would have paid thousands of dollars for it.

dearth.definition: a scarcity or lack of something
sentences: A dearth of qualified teachers in rural districts forced several schools to combine classes and cancel advanced courses altogether.
The critic lamented the dearth of original ideas in recent films, most of which were sequels or remakes of older movies.
dearth.mnemonic: Dearth ressemble à « death » : le manque, c'est presque la mort.

paucity.definition: smallness of number or quantity; scarcity
sentences: The paucity of reliable data made it impossible for the researchers to draw any firm conclusions about the drug's effectiveness.
Despite the paucity of her income, she managed to save a little each month by cooking at home and walking to work.
paucity.mnemonic: Même racine que « peu » / « pauvre » (latin paucus).

shortfall.definition: a deficit; the amount by which something falls short of what is needed
sentences: The university faced a budget shortfall of two million dollars after enrollment dropped, and administrators were forced to freeze all hiring.
To cover the shortfall in grain production caused by the floods, the country had to import thousands of tons of wheat.
After the bankruptcy of his firm, the once wealthy merchant lived in penury, unable to afford even a decent meal.
Many of the great composers died in penury, their genius recognized only long after they had passed away without any money.
penury.mnemonic: Proche de « pénurie » en français : c'est le manque d'argent extrême.

thrifty.definition: careful and wise in the use of money and resources
sentences: Raised by thrifty parents who saved every spare coin, she learned early to compare prices and never waste food.
The thrifty shopkeeper reused packaging and repaired old equipment rather than buying new, and over the years his savings grew considerably.

sparing.definition: restrained and economical in using or giving something
sentences: The coach was sparing in his praise, so when he finally told the young runner she had done well, she was thrilled.
Because water was scarce on the expedition, the guide urged everyone to be sparing in washing and to drink only what they needed.

spare.definition: plain and simple, without unnecessary detail; also, extra or left over
sentences: The poet's spare style, stripped of ornament and adjectives, achieves its power through a few carefully chosen words.
Since he had no spare time during the week, the busy surgeon reserved his weekends for gardening and reading with his children.

squander.definition: to waste something, such as money or opportunities, foolishly
sentences: The heir managed to squander his entire inheritance within five years, spending it on racehorses, parties, and a series of failed ventures.
By refusing to prepare for the exam, she would squander the opportunity that her teachers had worked so hard to give her.

spendthrift.definition: a person who spends money recklessly and wastefully
sentences: Her brother was a notorious spendthrift who bought expensive gadgets every week and was always borrowing money before the end of the month.
Unlike the careful saver in the family, the spendthrift emptied his bank account on a luxury watch he rarely wore.
spendthrift.mnemonic: Spend + thrift (économie) : celui qui dépense l'épargne.

profligate.definition: recklessly extravagant, or shamelessly immoral in behavior
sentences: The king's profligate lifestyle, with its endless banquets and gambling, drained the royal treasury and left the kingdom deeply in debt.
Moralists condemned the profligate nobleman, who squandered his fortune and was notorious for scandalous behavior throughout the capital.
The billionaire threw a lavish wedding, with imported flowers, a famous orchestra, and a banquet that lasted until dawn.
Reviewers gave lavish praise to the debut novel, calling it the most remarkable first book that they had read in years.

acquisitive.definition: eager to acquire money, possessions, or property
sentences: The acquisitive young executive was never satisfied, constantly buying more companies and properties in his hunt for greater wealth.
Critics described the museum's director as acquisitive, since he was always seeking to add new paintings to a collection already too large to display.
acquisitive.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « acquis » mais qui veut acquérir toujours plus.

embezzle.definition: to steal money entrusted to one's care, especially from an employer
sentences: The treasurer was arrested for trying to embezzle thousands of dollars from the charity, which he had been secretly transferring to his own account.
Auditors discovered that the accountant had been embezzling small sums for years, hiding the missing money through false entries in the company's ledgers.

parlay.definition: to turn an initial advantage or sum into something much greater
parlay.definitionFr: transformer un atout en gain plus grand
sentences: She managed to parlay a small inheritance into a large fortune by investing wisely in real estate throughout the 1990s.
The actor hoped to parlay his success in a minor television role into a career in films, and he soon won a leading part.
The mayor's decision to close the library provoked the ire of local residents, who gathered outside city hall to shout their protest.
Her ire was evident in her trembling voice and clenched fists when she learned that her colleague had taken credit for her work.
ire.mnemonic: Ire = « ire » du latin ira, comme « irascible ».

animus.definition: strong hostility or ill will, often deep-seated
sentences: The two rival families had felt such animus toward one another for generations that nobody could remember how the quarrel had begun.
The judge had to recuse himself because his obvious animus against the defendant would have made a fair trial impossible.

enmity.definition: deep-rooted and lasting hatred or hostility between people
sentences: The enmity between the neighboring countries lasted for centuries, surviving treaties, royal marriages, and several changes of government.
Their friendship turned to bitter enmity after the business partner betrayed him, and the two men never spoke again.

umbrage.definition: offense or resentment at a perceived slight
sentences: The senator took umbrage at the suggestion that he had been bribed, and he demanded an immediate apology from the reporter.
She took umbrage at her colleague's offhand remark about her age, and she left the meeting early without saying a word.
umbrage.mnemonic: Du latin umbra, l'ombre : on se sent « ombragé », vexé. Cf. ombrageux.

strife.definition: bitter conflict or discord between people or groups
sentences: Years of civil strife left the country divided and impoverished, with rival factions fighting over the capital and the best farmland.
The family business was torn by strife after the founder's death, as his children quarreled openly over who should lead the firm.

inimical.definition: hostile, or harmful and unfavorable in effect
sentences: Dictatorships are inimical to free speech, since leaders who fear criticism usually silence writers, journalists, and anyone who disagrees with them.
The harsh, dry climate proved inimical to the settlers' crops, and within two seasons most of the colony's farms had failed.
inimical.mnemonic: Même racine que « inimitié » et « ennemi ».

spiteful.definition: motivated by a desire to hurt or annoy someone out of malice
sentences: In a spiteful act of revenge, she deleted her former partner's files, knowing that the loss would cause him serious trouble.
The spiteful neighbor deliberately played loud music late at night, hoping to annoy the family who had complained about his dog.

treacherous.definition: betraying trust; also, hazardous and deceptively dangerous
sentences: The treacherous minister secretly sold state secrets to the enemy while publicly swearing loyalty to the king he was serving.
Icy patches made the mountain road treacherous, and several drivers who had trusted its apparently dry surface skidded off the edge.
It began to irk her that her roommate never washed the dishes, and eventually she posted a stern note on the refrigerator.
Nothing seemed to irk the teacher more than students who arrived late and then loudly interrupted the lesson to ask what they had missed.

rankle.definition: to cause lingering resentment or bitterness
rankle.definitionFr: rester en travers de la gorge
sentences: The unfair criticism continued to rankle long after the meeting ended, and she found herself repeating the insult in her mind all week.
It still rankles the veteran player that the club chose a younger rival for the captaincy, despite his years of loyal service.

nettlesome.definition: causing irritation or annoyance; troublesome and difficult
sentences: The nettlesome problem of funding for the bridge divided the council for months, and each proposed solution created fresh complaints.
He found the constant interruptions from his younger cousin nettlesome, as they kept him from finishing his essay before the deadline.
nettlesome.mnemonic: Nettle = ortie : une situation qui pique comme une ortie.

harrow.definition: to cause acute mental distress; to torment
sentences: The documentary about the refugees' long journey was so harrowing that many viewers left the theater in tears and unable to speak.
Memories of the accident continued to harrow him for years, and he often woke at night with his heart pounding.
harrow.mnemonic: Une herse (harrow) déchire la terre : on déchire l'âme.

sentences: It would be churlish to refuse the invitation after our hosts went to such trouble, so we accepted with a smile.
The churlish shopkeeper grunted at customers and slammed the cash drawer, and soon most regulars were going elsewhere.

boorish.definition: rude, insensitive, and lacking in manners or refinement
sentences: His boorish behavior at the formal dinner, which included belching loudly and insulting the hostess, left the other guests appalled.
The boorish tourist shouted at the waiter and ignored local customs, which embarrassed his companions and offended everyone in the restaurant.

crass.definition: crude and insensitive; lacking refinement or sensitivity
sentences: Mourners were shocked by his crass remark about the inheritance, made only minutes after the funeral had ended.
The advertisement was so crass in its exploitation of the tragedy that public outrage forced the company to withdraw it.
crass.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « crasse » (saleté) mais grossier dans les manières.

brash.definition: self-assertive in a rude, tactless, and overconfident way
sentences: The brash young lawyer interrupted senior partners and boasted about his victories, and his lack of tact made enemies quickly.
Her brash prediction that she would defeat the champion in the first round amused the crowd, but it also made her a target.
In a brazen robbery, the thieves walked into the gallery at noon and carried out the painting while the guards watched.
He told a brazen lie, looking the judge straight in the eye and showing no sign of embarrassment about the evidence against him.

unseemly.definition: not proper or appropriate for the occasion; improper
sentences: Laughing loudly at the funeral struck the mourners as unseemly, and several relatives frowned at him until he fell silent.
The senator regarded it as unseemly for officials to haggle over their salaries while the city's schools were short of money.

impolitic.definition: unwise and tactless; poorly judged for the circumstances
sentences: It was impolitic of the candidate to criticize the region's main industry while campaigning in a town that depended on it for jobs.
The ambassador's impolitic joke about the host country's cuisine nearly caused a diplomatic incident and forced the minister to apologize.
impolitic.mnemonic: Im + politic : le contraire de politique, sans tact diplomatique.

flippant.definition: showing a lack of proper respect or seriousness
sentences: The judge was angered by the defendant's flippant answers, which treated the serious charges as though they were a joke.
Her flippant reply to the question about the budget crisis suggested that she did not understand how grave the situation was.
flippant.mnemonic: Faux ami : rien à voir avec « flipper » ; c'est la désinvolture.

facetious.definition: treating serious matters with inappropriate humor; jokingly
sentences: The professor's facetious comment during the solemn ceremony drew a few nervous laughs but earned a stern look from the dean.
Please don't be facetious; this is a serious question, and I need a real answer rather than another joke.
facetious.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « facétieux » au sens aimable, mais plaisanterie déplacée.

diffident.definition: modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence
sentences: The diffident young scientist spoke so quietly during her presentation that the audience could hardly hear her important results.
Though brilliant, he was diffident about his talents and rarely offered his opinions unless the group specifically asked for them.
diffident.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « différent » mais « dé-fiant » : sans confiance en soi.

coy.definition: pretending to be shy or reluctant, often to tease
sentences: When reporters asked whether she would run for office, the senator gave a coy smile and refused to give a direct answer.
The company remained coy about its new product, hinting at a launch date without revealing a single technical detail.

reticent.definition: reluctant to speak about one's thoughts or feelings; reserved
sentences: The witness was reticent about the details of the incident, answering questions in single words and avoiding the lawyer's gaze.
Normally talkative, he became reticent when asked about his childhood, changing the subject whenever the conversation turned to his family.
reticent.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « réticent » (hésitant à agir) mais réservé à parler.

wary.definition: cautious about possible dangers or problems
sentences: After being cheated once, the traveler grew wary of strangers who offered help and checked every price before agreeing to pay.
Investors remain wary of the new technology, since several similar ventures collapsed within a year of attracting millions in funding.

chary.definition: cautious and reluctant to give or risk something
sentences: Having lost money before, the banker was chary of lending to new businesses and demanded extensive guarantees from every applicant.
The famous author was chary of granting interviews, fearing that reporters would distort his words and invade his private life.
The skittish horse bolted at the slightest noise, so the rider had to speak softly and keep a firm grip on the reins.
Skittish investors sold their shares at the first rumor of trouble, causing the market to fall even though the company was sound.
The craven soldier threw down his weapon and fled at the first sound of gunfire, leaving his comrades to face the enemy alone.
Critics denounced the craven politician who, afraid of public anger, abandoned his principles and voted against the bill he had promised to support.

foolhardy.definition: recklessly bold; taking risks without sensible thought
sentences: It was foolhardy to attempt to cross the frozen lake in spring, and the hikers narrowly escaped when the ice cracked beneath them.
The foolhardy investor put all his savings into a single unproven start-up, ignoring warnings from every financial adviser he consulted.
